description: Combat, enemy AI and weapon systems on a toy-themed souls-like at Luski Game Studio.

Page draft for the portfolio. Lines marked ASSET are things for you to find; brackets are facts to confirm.

Souls-like / Action-Adventure · Luski Game Studio · Canceled

Designed the weapon system and around 10 of 15 enemy archetypes for a toy-themed souls-like, balanced with a hits-to-kill model.

At a glance: 15 enemy archetypes, around 10 designed by me · \[6\] enemy design rules · 3-way damage-type system · weapon types cut from 4 to 3

ASSET – Hero video (most important): 45–60 seconds of combat against 2–3 different archetypes, ideally showing a weapon swap that changes how a fight goes. Prototype footage is fine for a canceled game; label it "prototype".

• What I owned: the weapon system and damage types, around 10 enemy archetypes, progression and the economy, and the balancing spreadsheets.
  • Hardest problem: four weapon types made the team's enemy production too big for its size. Cutting one type kept the variety and saved the scope.
  • What it shows: combat systems built from rules, and treating scope as a design decision.

blocks.html:
A satirical souls-like set in a world of cursed toys. Players explore, fight demanding enemies and boss fights, and grow their character through weapons, items and progression. Combat rewards learning each enemy and choosing the right weapon for it.

ASSET – 3–4 screenshots: an enemy lineup or concept sheet, a combat moment, a weapon selection screen, the character creator.

• A small indie team \[of about 10\], so every enemy, weapon and animation had a real production cost.
  • Souls-like expectations: fights need to be hard but fair, and readable enough that players blame themselves, not the game.
  • Toy-themed enemies had unusual silhouettes and physics-driven movement, which made readability harder.

1. Readable at a glance. Players identify an enemy's type and threat from its silhouette and movement.
  2. The right weapon matters, but never locks you out. Switching weapons is rewarded; sticking with one is never a dead end.
  3. Hard but fair. Difficulty comes from learning patterns, not from hidden numbers.

[Confirm these match the pillars the team used, or replace them with yours.\]

The goal was enemies that read clearly at a glance and play differently from each other, using odd toy silhouettes and physics-driven movement. With 15 archetypes on a small team, I set the rules before designing any enemy, so every new one fit the same standard.

[embedded content: enemy design process · 5 steps\]

blocks.text: The rules every archetype had to meet

rows: **Clear contrast:** its own silhouette and movement
**Swarm caps:** a population limit for swarm enemies
**Hit-stop by weight:** impact pause scales with mass and speed
Heavy hits feel heavy, light ones stay snappy

blocks.html: [Fill in the other three rules, or change the headline count to 3.\]

Some archetypes were later cut for animation or readability limits; mark which ones.

ASSET – Enemy lineup: concept art or silhouettes of the archetypes side by side. A silhouette lineup proves the "clear contrast" rule in one image.

ASSET – One enemy spec sheet: a page from your character stat document (linked on Wix) for one archetype you designed.

Each weapon type leans toward one of three damage types, and each enemy is strong or weak against them. For example, a slashing weapon deals extra damage to cloth enemies. Players are rewarded for switching weapons without being locked into one loadout.

  • Mixed damage: every weapon deals all three damage types at different percentages, so no enemy is ever fully immune to what the player is holding.
  • Specialise without losing flexibility: upgrades let players invest deeply in one damage type while every weapon stays useful.
  • Weapon feel: types differ in reach, attack timing, stamina cost, moveset and damage.

ASSET – Damage triangle (on the Wix page; update its labels with the final damage types first).

ASSET – Weapon type table: one row per type, with reach, speed, stamina cost and strong-against. This is quick to build from your spreadsheet and shows the system's shape at once.

I built damage calculators and a hits-to-kill matrix in spreadsheets: how many strikes each weapon needs against each archetype. It made progression predictable and showed unfair matchups before they reached the engine.

ASSET – Hits-to-kill matrix screenshot: weapons down the side, archetypes across the top, colour-coded. Readers who never open your spreadsheet will still see the method.

blocks.text: Iteration case 1: cutting a weapon type to protect scope

blocks.html:
[embedded content: iteration case 1 · before and after\]

Problem: four weapon types made combat interesting, but every type needed enemies that tested it. The number of enemies the team would have to produce grew beyond what a small team could make.

Fix: I cut one weapon type, going from 4 to 3, and added more weapons within each remaining type.

Result: fewer enemies to produce, and each one could be harder and more interesting, while weapon variety stayed high. \[Add numbers if you have them: enemies planned before and after, weapons per type.\]

• Problem: \[what playtesters said or did\]
  • Fix: I co-designed a stamina mechanic \[how it works: what costs stamina, how it recovers\].
  • Result: \[how fights changed\]

• Climb mechanic: designed with level design and engineering to solve level layout problems. \[What problem did it solve?\]
  • Boss fight: designed with game design, level design and engineering. ASSET: a boss concept or arena sketch.
  • Character creation: designed the system and its UI in Adobe XD with UI and engineering. ASSET: one Adobe XD screen.
  • Progression and economy: designed player and item progression and the economy.

• Fewer weapon types, deeper enemies. Less breadth in the arsenal, but a roster the team could actually build.
  • Mixed damage over hard counters. Weaker "perfect counter" moments, but no fight ever becomes impossible with the wrong weapon.
  • Rules before roster. Slower to start, but 15 archetypes stayed consistent and readable.
The game was canceled before release. The weapon system, damage matrix and enemy standards were \[implemented in the prototype / documented only; confirm which\].

What worked: writing the enemy rules first, and modelling hits-to-kill before building fights.

What I'd do differently: \[pick what's true, for example: check content cost earlier, before designing four weapon types\].

What I learned: in combat systems, every new option multiplies the content needed elsewhere, so scope is a design decision too.
